frontmatter_description: Diagnose regret, relief, disappointment, or pleasant surprise by comparing what happened with a salient alternative outcome.
title: Counterfactual Emotion
use_when: Use when the question asks what emotion follows from comparing reality with a salient alternative outcome.
Use when the answer depends on whether the actual outcome feels better or worse than what could have happened.
Use when the scene is about regret, relief, disappointment, or pleasant surprise from a contrast case, not from responsibility or norm violation.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the emotion is explained by blame, guilt, shame, pride, anger, or gratitude tied to responsibility or moral appraisal.
Do not use when the issue is simple success, failure, happiness, or sadness with no explicit or implied alternative outcome.
Do not use when the main question is outward display, suppression, empathy, or emotion regulation rather than the felt emotion itself.
Do not use when the comparison is about probability, certainty, or evidence alone without an emotional counterfactual contrast.
decision_variable: actual outcome versus salient alternative outcome
trigger_checklist: Is there a clear actual outcome?
Is there a plausible alternative outcome that matters to the character?
Is the emotion based on comparing those two outcomes?
Is the alternative better or worse than reality from the character's point of view?
Is the target emotion regret, relief, disappointment, or pleasant surprise?
workflow: Identify the real outcome that occurred.
Identify the salient alternative outcome that could have happened.
Compare the two outcomes from the character's perspective.
Infer the emotion from the direction of the comparison.
If no contrast is doing the work, exit to a different emotion skill.

special_case.title: Implied alternative, not stated alternative
special_case.rule: Use this unit even when the alternative is only implied, as long as the emotional answer depends on 'could have happened' contrast rather than on blame, norm, or display.

worked_example.scene: A driver narrowly avoids a crash and then goes quiet.
worked_example.question: What does the driver most likely feel?
worked_example.answer_logic: The actual outcome is much better than the feared alternative of crashing, so the emotion is relief.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit to micro-26 Basic Emotion Appraisal if the question can be answered without comparing reality to an alternative outcome.
Exit to micro-30 Moral Emotion if responsibility, wrongdoing, or social norm is the main cause of the emotion.
Exit to micro-28 Hidden Emotion or micro-29 Emotional Disguise if the task asks how the person shows, hides, or manages the emotion rather than what the emotion is.
Exit to micro-33 Emotion Regulation if the question is about coping with or reframing the emotion after it arises.

references.route_signal: Route here when the scene asks for regret, relief, disappointment, or pleasant surprise based on a better-or-worse alternative outcome.
hard_boundary: The deciding cue must be a salient alternative outcome the character contrasts with reality; without that contrast, ordinary appraisal (micro-26) handles the emotion.
If guilt, shame, pride, anger, or gratitude depends on responsibility or norm violation, route to micro-30 Moral Emotion even when the outcome was bad.
The unit reads the felt emotion (regret, relief, disappointment, pleasant surprise); how the character shows or copes with it belongs to micro-29 or micro-33.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not label any bad outcome as regret by default.
Do not confuse disappointment with simple sadness.
Do not infer relief unless the character is comparing the actual outcome with a worse possible outcome.
common_failure_modes: Answering with a generic positive or negative emotion instead of the counterfactual one.
Using blame or morality when the scene is only about outcome comparison.
Missing implied alternatives and treating the scene as plain success or failure.

minimal_pair.case: A student misses the deadline by one minute and thinks about how submitting on time would have avoided the zero.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The emotion depends on comparing the actual bad outcome with a better possible outcome, which supports regret or disappointment.

minimal_pair.case: A patient learns the test was negative after fearing it might be positive.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: The actual outcome is better than the feared alternative, so the emotion is relief.

boundary_stress_test: If the character feels bad because they were careless, ask whether blame is driving the answer; if yes, exit to moral emotion.
If the character is simply sad about a loss with no meaningful alternative, do not use this unit.
If the scene mentions 'should have' but the question is really about shame or guilt, do not force a counterfactual reading.
references.generalization_note: This unit is about emotional contrast, not outcome quality alone: use it only when the comparison with an alternative outcome changes the emotion label.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: The character evaluates what happened against a better or worse alternative and feels regret, relief, disappointment, or pleasant surprise.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: The character has a positive or negative feeling, but no alternative outcome is part of the reasoning.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The character feels guilt, pride, or shame because of fault, praise, or norm violation.

notes: Keep the focus on the contrast between actual and alternative outcomes.
This is a diagnostic micro skill, not a full scene template.
Pleasant surprise belongs here only when it is the emotional result of a better-than-alternative outcome.
core_question: Infer regret, relief, disappointment, or pleasant surprise from comparison with an alternative outcome
